question.text: A PM's portfolio has a max drawdown of 22% over the last 5 years. This means:

answer.text: The portfolio lost exactly 22% on one day
The largest peak-to-trough decline in portfolio NAV was 22%

explanation.text: The Logic: Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall in a portfolio's NAV over the observation window, expressed as a percentage of the prior peak. A 22% max drawdown over 5 years means that, at some point in that window, NAV fell 22% from its highest preceding level before recovering — it captures the worst realised pain, not a single-day move or a forward-looking risk estimate. The Trap: A 22% one-day loss is a specific daily return, not a peak-to-trough span; volatility is the standard deviation of returns, a different statistical concept; 'expected loss' is a forward-looking probabilistic measure, not a backward-looking maximum. Note: The NISM-Series-XXI-B workbook chapter on risk (pp. 293-300 and 371-379) covers VaR, stress testing, liquidity risk, credit risk and black-swan preparedness, but does not define maximum drawdown / peak-to-trough decline in the pages checked. The definition above is the standard industry usage of the term.
